title: Short Stuff: Curse of Broken Mirrors
summary: Short Stuff episode on the superstition that breaking a mirror brings seven years of bad luck. The hosts trace mirror lore from ancient Greek Narcissus myth and Roman polished-metal mirrors (shields) to the idea that mirror reflections held the soul, the seven-year explanation (Roman life cycles or the cost of a mirror equaling seven years of servant wages), and the first English-language mention in 1777. They cover ways to mitigate bad luck such as disposing of broken pieces safely and burying them under a full moon, plus other mirror and glass superstitions: covering mirrors after a death, souls trapped in mirrors, demons escaping through mirrors, Edwardian candlelight mirror divination about future husbands, post-wedding mirror superstitions, and glass-breaking customs.

segments.title: Intro and mirror superstition setup
segments.summary: The hosts introduce the episode on the belief that breaking a mirror brings seven years of bad luck, noting an earlier episode touched on mirrors.

segments.title: Narcissus and early Greek and Roman mirror beliefs
segments.summary: The Greeks linked seeing one's reflection with danger via the Narcissus myth. The Romans shared similar beliefs and made mirrors from highly polished metal, such as shields.

segments.title: Digression on Narcissus pronunciation and Lucy Wainwright Roche
segments.summary: The hosts discuss how to pronounce Narcissus and mention Lucy Wainwright Roche touring with the Indigo Girls. This is off-topic banter.

segments.title: Mirrors as souls and the reasons breaking one causes misfortune
segments.summary: Mirrors were thought to let gods observe souls, so breaking one was disrespectful and could anger gods. Belief held that breaking a mirror breaks the soul, which can leave the body unprotected for seven years or take revenge by killing a loved one.

segments.title: Origins of the seven-year figure
segments.summary: The seven-year period may come from Roman beliefs in seven-year life cycles, or from mirrors being so expensive that one cost seven years of a servant's work. The hosts say both could be true.

segments.title: First English mention in 1777 and spread in British culture
segments.summary: The first English-language mention of breaking a mirror as bad luck dates to 1777, linking mirrors to divination used by magicians. Being in print spread the belief in British culture.

segments.title: Disposing of broken mirror pieces and burying them under a full moon
segments.summary: Advice to remove broken mirror pieces quickly, wrapped in paper or a cardboard box since sharp glass cuts plastic bags. Burying them under a full moon is discussed; the hosts joke about storing pieces for a month and agree on a two-day window.

segments.title: Grinding mirror into powder and throwing salt
segments.summary: Joking advice to grind the mirror into powder and throw salt over the left shoulder to get rid of bad luck.
topics: good luck and bad luck folklore

segments.title: Glass-breaking customs and other mirror superstitions
segments.summary: Breaking non-mirror glass can be good luck, or a death omen in England. Greek celebrations and Jewish weddings involve breaking glass to ward off evil spirits. Covering mirrors after a death is discussed, since the soul could get stuck in a mirror.

segments.title: Mirrors, the dead, and tarnishing
segments.summary: Covering mirrors after death is linked to the belief that the mirror tarnishes or shows the deceased. The hosts joke about the consequences of a broken mirror.

segments.title: Demons escaping through mirrors
segments.summary: Some people believed demons could pass through mirrors from the non-living world into the living world, which is another reason to cover mirrors after a death.

segments.title: Edwardian candlelight mirror divination and wedding superstition
segments.summary: In Edwardian Britain (1901 to 1910), a person could sit before a mirror by candlelight to see a future husband, or a grim specter signaling they would die unmarried. A post-wedding superstition says looking into a mirror after saying I do unites the couple's souls in an alternate universe.

segments.title: Closing banter and sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts joke about kissing mirrors for Halloween and end the episode with the iHeartRadio credit and a pointer to other podcasts.
